posts.cooked:
Hi Elias,

I can build this for you. I work with n8n daily and have built multi-platform API publishing systems, CRM-to-social pipelines, and large-scale automation workflows that handle token management, error recovery, and credential rotation across dozens of accounts. This is exactly the kind of architecture I specialize in.

Before jumping into the build, here are the technical realities that will determine whether this system actually holds at scale or breaks at account 20. Most replies in this thread haven’t addressed these, and they’re the difference between a workflow that works for a demo and one that runs reliably across 300 accounts.

Instagram publishing through the Graph API requires the video to be hosted at a publicly accessible URL. Google Drive links don’t work directly because Meta’s servers need to fetch the video from a URL they can reach. The workflow needs to either generate a temporary public link from Drive, or push the file to a staging endpoint (like a temporary cloud storage URL) that Meta can pull from. Without this step, every single Instagram post will fail silently with no error message. I’d build this as an automatic step in the workflow so you never have to think about it.

Meta long-lived tokens expire after 60 days, and short-lived tokens expire in 1 hour. For 1-3 accounts that’s a minor inconvenience. At 100+ accounts, if you don’t have automated token refresh built into the workflow, you’ll wake up one morning and 40 accounts will have been dark for a week with zero notification. I’d build a token health check that runs before every publishing cycle. It validates each account’s token, attempts an automatic refresh if it’s close to expiry, and sends you a Telegram alert with the exact account name and platform if a refresh fails. That way you fix it before it affects publishing, not after.

YouTube’s Data API has a default quota of 10,000 units per day, and each video upload costs 1,600 units. That’s roughly 6 uploads per day across ALL channels on a single Google Cloud project. At 300 accounts, you’d burn through the entire daily quota on just 6 videos. You need a quota increase from Google, which requires an application explaining your use case and approval from their team. This needs to happen before the scale-up, not during it. I can guide you through that application and structure the workflow to work within whatever quota ceiling you get, including spreading uploads across multiple API projects if needed.

Rate limiting and bot detection across platforms. If the workflow fires 100 posts to Meta simultaneously, you’ll get rate-limited or flagged. The same goes for YouTube. I’d build the publishing with staggered delays between accounts, randomized timing intervals, and per-platform queue management so each post goes out in a natural pattern. This is the part most people skip, and it’s the reason most scaled social posting systems get accounts restricted.

For the architecture, I’d structure it as a parent-child workflow system:

  • Parent workflow watches your Google Drive folder for new video files using the Drive trigger node
  • On detecting a new file, it reads the caption Sheet, matches the video filename to the correct row, and pulls the caption text plus all target account credentials from that row
  • It then spawns child workflow executions for each account, passing the video file, caption, and that account’s specific API credentials
  • Each child execution handles the actual publishing to one platform for one account, with its own retry logic, error handling, and status logging
  • A results Sheet logs every single publish attempt: account name, platform, video filename, timestamp, success/failure, error message if any, and the post ID/URL if successful. At 300 accounts, this audit trail is how you know what actually went out.

Additional things I’d build into the system:

  • Duplicate upload detection so re-uploading or renaming a video file doesn’t trigger double posts across all accounts
  • Per-account status tracking in the Sheet itself, so you can see at a glance which accounts are active, which have token issues, and which had failed posts
  • Telegram notification system with separate alerts for successes (daily summary of what posted where) and failures (immediate alert with the specific account, platform, and error reason)
  • A “pause” column in the Sheet so you can temporarily disable publishing to any account without removing its credentials

A few things worth clarifying on scope, since the answers will shape how the system gets built:

  1. Are the 300 accounts all yours, or do they belong to clients? If they’re client accounts, Meta requires Business Verification and App Review for managing third-party pages and Instagram accounts through the API. That’s a separate approval process with its own timeline.
  2. Do all 300 accounts get the same video with the same caption, or do different accounts get different content? If some accounts are segmented by niche or language, the Sheet structure and the matching logic change significantly.
  3. Is the posting schedule the same for all accounts (post immediately on upload), or do different accounts post at different times? If you want timezone-optimized posting or staggered scheduling, that’s a different layer.
  4. Do you need the system to handle different video formats or aspect ratios per platform? Instagram Reels, Facebook feed videos, and YouTube uploads have different spec requirements. If you’re uploading one video that needs to go everywhere, we might need a formatting/transcoding step.
  5. What’s your n8n hosting situation? Self-hosted or n8n Cloud? At 300 accounts per video upload, the execution volume is substantial. Self-hosted on a decent server would handle it, but n8n Cloud on certain plans has execution limits that could become a bottleneck.

I’m happy to start with the 1-3 account test, deliver it fully working with the walkthrough video, and structure it so the scale-up to 300 is an expansion of the same architecture rather than a rebuild. DM me and we can sort out the details.

Hi Elias,

I can build this for you. I work with n8n daily and have built multi-platform API publishing systems, CRM-to-social pipelines, and large-scale automation workflows that handle token management, error recovery, and credential rotation across dozens of accounts. This is exactly the kind of architecture I specialize in.

Before jumping into the build, here are the technical realities that will determine whether this system actually holds at scale or breaks at account 20. Most replies in this thread haven’t addressed these, and they’re the difference between a workflow that works for a demo and one that runs reliably across 300 accounts.

Instagram publishing through the Graph API requires the video to be hosted at a publicly accessible URL. Google Drive links don’t work directly because Meta’s servers need to fetch the video from a URL they can reach. The workflow needs to either generate a temporary public link from Drive, or push the file to a staging endpoint (like a temporary cloud storage URL) that Meta can pull from. Without this step, every single Instagram post will fail silently with no error message. I’d build this as an automatic step in the workflow so you never have to think about it.

Meta long-lived tokens expire after 60 days, and short-lived tokens expire in 1 hour. For 1-3 accounts that’s a minor inconvenience. At 100+ accounts, if you don’t have automated token refresh built into the workflow, you’ll wake up one morning and 40 accounts will have been dark for a week with zero notification. I’d build a token health check that runs before every publishing cycle. It validates each account’s token, attempts an automatic refresh if it’s close to expiry, and sends you a Telegram alert with the exact account name and platform if a refresh fails. That way you fix it before it affects publishing, not after.

YouTube’s Data API has a default quota of 10,000 units per day, and each video upload costs 1,600 units. That’s roughly 6 uploads per day across ALL channels on a single Google Cloud project. At 300 accounts, you’d burn through the entire daily quota on just 6 videos. You need a quota increase from Google, which requires an application explaining your use case and approval from their team. This needs to happen before the scale-up, not during it. I can guide you through that application and structure the workflow to work within whatever quota ceiling you get, including spreading uploads across multiple API projects if needed.

Rate limiting and bot detection across platforms. If the workflow fires 100 posts to Meta simultaneously, you’ll get rate-limited or flagged. The same goes for YouTube. I’d build the publishing with staggered delays between accounts, randomized timing intervals, and per-platform queue management so each post goes out in a natural pattern. This is the part most people skip, and it’s the reason most scaled social posting systems get accounts restricted.

For the architecture, I’d structure it as a parent-child workflow system:

  • Parent workflow watches your Google Drive folder for new video files using the Drive trigger node
  • On detecting a new file, it reads the caption Sheet, matches the video filename to the correct row, and pulls the caption text plus all target account credentials from that row
  • It then spawns child workflow executions for each account, passing the video file, caption, and that account’s specific API credentials
  • Each child execution handles the actual publishing to one platform for one account, with its own retry logic, error handling, and status logging
  • A results Sheet logs every single publish attempt: account name, platform, video filename, timestamp, success/failure, error message if any, and the post ID/URL if successful. At 300 accounts, this audit trail is how you know what actually went out.

Additional things I’d build into the system:

  • Duplicate upload detection so re-uploading or renaming a video file doesn’t trigger double posts across all accounts
  • Per-account status tracking in the Sheet itself, so you can see at a glance which accounts are active, which have token issues, and which had failed posts
  • Telegram notification system with separate alerts for successes (daily summary of what posted where) and failures (immediate alert with the specific account, platform, and error reason)
  • A “pause” column in the Sheet so you can temporarily disable publishing to any account without removing its credentials

A few things worth clarifying on scope, since the answers will shape how the system gets built:

  1. Are the 300 accounts all yours, or do they belong to clients? If they’re client accounts, Meta requires Business Verification and App Review for managing third-party pages and Instagram accounts through the API. That’s a separate approval process with its own timeline.
  2. Do all 300 accounts get the same video with the same caption, or do different accounts get different content? If some accounts are segmented by niche or language, the Sheet structure and the matching logic change significantly.
  3. Is the posting schedule the same for all accounts (post immediately on upload), or do different accounts post at different times? If you want timezone-optimized posting or staggered scheduling, that’s a different layer.
  4. Do you need the system to handle different video formats or aspect ratios per platform? Instagram Reels, Facebook feed videos, and YouTube uploads have different spec requirements. If you’re uploading one video that needs to go everywhere, we might need a formatting/transcoding step.
  5. What’s your n8n hosting situation? Self-hosted or n8n Cloud? At 300 accounts per video upload, the execution volume is substantial. Self-hosted on a decent server would handle it, but n8n Cloud on certain plans has execution limits that could become a bottleneck.

I work with n8n daily and have built multi-platform API publishing systems, CRM-to-social pipelines, and large-scale automation workflows that handle token management, error recovery, and credential rotation across dozens of accounts. This is exactly the kind of architecture I specialize in. 
 Before jumping into the build, here are the technical realities that will determine whether this system actually holds at scale or breaks at account 20. Most replies in this thread haven’t addressed these, and they’re the difference between a workflow that works for a demo and one that runs reliably across 300 accounts. 
  Instagram publishing through the Graph API requires the video to be hosted at a publicly accessible URL.  Google Drive links don’t work directly because Meta’s servers need to fetch the video from a URL they can reach. The workflow needs to either generate a temporary public link from Drive, or push the file to a staging endpoint (like a temporary cloud storage URL) that Meta can pull from. Without this step, every single Instagram post will fail silently with no error message. I’d build this as an automatic step in the workflow so you never have to think about it. 
  Meta long-lived tokens expire after 60 days, and short-lived tokens expire in 1 hour.  For 1-3 accounts that’s a minor inconvenience. At 100+ accounts, if you don’t have automated token refresh built into the workflow, you’ll wake up one morning and 40 accounts will have been dark for a week with zero notification. I’d build a token health check that runs before every publishing cycle. It validates each account’s token, attempts an automatic refresh if it’s close to expiry, and sends you a Telegram alert with the exact account name and platform if a refresh fails. That way you fix it before it affects publishing, not after. 
  YouTube’s Data API has a default quota of 10,000 units per day, and each video upload costs 1,600 units.  That’s roughly 6 uploads per day across ALL channels on a single Google Cloud project. At 300 accounts, you’d burn through the entire daily quota on just 6 videos. You need a quota increase from Google, which requires an application explaining your use case and approval from their team. This needs to happen before the scale-up, not during it. I can guide you through that application and structure the workflow to work within whatever quota ceiling you get, including spreading uploads across multiple API projects if needed. 
  Rate limiting and bot detection across platforms.  If the workflow fires 100 posts to Meta simultaneously, you’ll get rate-limited or flagged. The same goes for YouTube. I’d build the publishing with staggered delays between accounts, randomized timing intervals, and per-platform queue management so each post goes out in a natural pattern. This is the part most people skip, and it’s the reason most scaled social posting systems get accounts restricted. 
  For the architecture , I’d structure it as a parent-child workflow system: 
 
  Parent workflow  watches your Google Drive folder for new video files using the Drive trigger node 
 On detecting a new file, it reads the caption Sheet, matches the video filename to the correct row, and pulls the caption text plus all target account credentials from that row 
 It then  spawns child workflow executions  for each account, passing the video file, caption, and that account’s specific API credentials 
 Each child execution handles the actual publishing to one platform for one account, with its own retry logic, error handling, and status logging 
 A  results Sheet  logs every single publish attempt: account name, platform, video filename, timestamp, success/failure, error message if any, and the post ID/URL if successful. At 300 accounts, this audit trail is how you know what actually went out. 
 
 Additional things I’d build into the system: 
 
  Duplicate upload detection  so re-uploading or renaming a video file doesn’t trigger double posts across all accounts 
  Per-account status tracking  in the Sheet itself, so you can see at a glance which accounts are active, which have token issues, and which had failed posts 
  Telegram notification system  with separate alerts for successes (daily summary of what posted where) and failures (immediate alert with the specific account, platform, and error reason) 
  A “pause” column  in the Sheet so you can temporarily disable publishing to any account without removing its credentials 
 
  A few things worth clarifying on scope , since the answers will shape how the system gets built: 
 
  Are the 300 accounts all yours, or do they belong to clients?  If they’re client accounts, Meta requires Business Verification and App Review for managing third-party pages and Instagram accounts through the API. That’s a separate approval process with its own timeline.

comments.author: Chineydu
comments.text:
Hi  @Elias_Rothschild  , I do not want to repeat what others have already told you about tokens and rate limits, so here are two things nobody in this thread has mentioned yet, and both decide whether your setup survives past the first week. 
 First, make your Google Sheet the control panel, not just the caption source. Add a status column for every account and platform, so each row can read queued, publishing, done, or failed with a short reason. The workflow only touches rows that are queued, writes publishing while it works, and finally writes done or the exact error. Because you do not code, this matters a lot. You can open the Sheet at any moment and see exactly what went out and what did not, and you can republish a single failed row yourself by setting it back to queued, without calling anyone. It also makes the whole thing restart safe. If n8n reboots midway, nothing gets posted twice, because the status column already knows what finished. 
 Second, add a preflight media check before any publishing happens. Instagram, Facebook and YouTube each reject different things: aspect ratio, clip length, codec, and file size limits are not the same across the three. If you skip this, the same video can post fine to YouTube and silently fail on Instagram, and you will not know why. One small validation step that reads the video properties and marks a row as failed with the reason, before it ever calls an API, saves you from burning attempts and from confusing partial failures. 
 On the 20 dollar test, my honest advice is to not judge it by whether one video posted once. Ask it to prove the hard part: one real account fully authorised, one real publish to each of the three platforms, and one deliberate failure that the system catches, logs, and lets you retry from the Sheet. If a build handles that cleanly at 1 to 3 accounts, it will scale. If it only shows a single happy path post, it tells you nothing about 300 accounts.
